articles.title: Taika Waititi Says It’s “Probably Inevitable” AI Will Be Used in Hollywood But It’s “Boring and Lame” to “Type in Prompts to Make a Movie”
articles.author: Kirsten Chuba

paras.en: Taika Waititi’s adaptation of Kazuo Ishiguro’s 2021 novel Klara and the Sun, starring Jenna Ortega and Amy Adams, was developed years before AI arrived in full force and the discussion about its potential permeated Hollywood. But at the film’s New York special screening on Monday, the team behind the movie told The Hollywood Reporter it’s a timely story that underscores the necessity of embracing our own humanity amid the rise of new technology and the power of human connection in and outside of the industry.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Ishiguro’s dystopian coming-of-age drama is set in a version of the future where people can “lift” their children, a process that genetically engineers them to have enhanced academic abilities. The drive to create more successful children also fuels an isolating society, leading to the development and creation of purchasable, solar-powered artificial intelligence known as Artificial Friends. Ortega portrays Klara, a slightly defective A.F. and the story’s narrator, brought home by Adams’ Chrissy for her daughter Josie (Mia Tharia), who has become sick since being lifted.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “What I love so much about this story, and why I wanted to do this story, is because yes, Klara is an Artificial Friend and she comes into this very broken, complicated family that really doesn’t communicate enough with one another. But by the end of the story, she allows them to appreciate one another’s flaws, to talk it out,” Ortega explained of her role. “In this very isolated, dark, weird, dystopian world, she brings them back to knowing love. And what has been so true in all these different centuries of being human, and at the core of everything, is that it is always about love, and it’s always going to be about love.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: For Waititi, who not only directed but also co-wrote the film with Dahvi Waller, he worked closely with Ishiguro on translating the popular novel for the screen.

“Right from the start, I talked to Ishiguro and said, ‘This is the kind of tone I’m looking for. This is the sort of thing I want to do,’ and he was so supportive. He said, ‘I don’t want you to do a faithful, super loyal adaptation of the book because that’s going to be boring. Every time someone tries to do that with my work, it doesn’t work out,’” Waititi said. “So he encouraged me to push it more in my direction.”

On Klara and the Sun, Waititi’s vision was informed by a history of telling stories led by younger protagonists, as well as his own life as a father. That helped him lean into what was on the page even when it diverged from it.

While there are many themes in Ishiguro’s novel, its most poignant touch upon the relationship between technology and humanity. Klara and the Sun is as much a conversation about how the development and use of technology, in particular ways, deteriorate Josie’s experience of being alive as it is about how robot friend Klara discovers the ways her own technology cannot and will not ever replicate the distinctly human experience.

“There’s this idea of being lifted and giving our children all of these advantages. But as it shows, there’s a great risk to that,” noted Adams. “In our story, the stakes are very heightened, but I think everything’s about the journey. This idea of chasing perfection, chasing achievement over chasing experience, is something that we have to examine.”

Ortega emphasized the message that sits at the heart of the book’s ending. “Artificial intelligence doesn’t feel love; it doesn’t know anything about it. It can be curious. It can try, but at the end of the day, it’s the people that we’re surrounded by that make life and living so special,” Ortega said.

When it comes to working on the film, its director, cast and studio leadership all underscored the power of human collaboration and creativity in bringing it to life. For Waititi, he “didn’t get into making film to sit by myself in a room and type in prompts to make a movie. That just seems so boring and lame to me. I want to interact with people.”

“You get spontaneity, and the mistakes and the things where you stumble through a performance, and you discover things through getting a line wrong or trying to fix up a line you’ve messed up. That’s what makes us so unique and so amazing: the ability to pivot and to use our mistakes to make something more interesting,” he continued. “I think robots are trained on all the successes and all the perfect stuff that humans have made. You’re not trained on the mistakes. There’s a big discussion about AI coming in: Will people use it? How much will they use it? I know it’s probably inevitable that we end up using it in our industry, but as long as it’s used by humans as a tool, as opposed to a replacement — I don’t want to replace humans. I want to work with them.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Added Adams, “The point of this movie and the novel is that the best that certain technology like AI can do is reflect ourselves back to us. It’s our responsibility to take the opportunity to see the best in each other. If used correctly, advancements in technology can do amazing things. But if used incorrectly, it can separate us. We’re at that threshold, and I really hope we choose each other.”
Klara and the Sun hits theaters on Friday.

articles.title: Trump sued over 50% tariffs on Canada in latest trade challenge

paras.en: A new lawsuit filed Tuesday challenges President Donald Trump's invocation of a Depression-era law to impose 50% tariffs on a range of Canadian goods.

Trump in July used Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 to slap those steep tariffs on Canadian hockey sticks, wine, honey, wigs, and other products in response to alleged trade discrimination by Ottawa. It was the first time the 96-year-old law had ever been used to impose a tariff.
"Section 338 is a relic of the retaliation-based tariff policy" that has been "impliedly repealed" by subsequent legislation, the civil complaint filed in the U.S. Court of International Trade says.

The suit was filed by Gellert Global Group, a New Jersey-based food importer that says its cheeses are covered by the tariffs. The complaint asks the court to declare the tariffs unlawful, block their enforcement, and order the Trump administration to issue refunds for duties already paid, with interest.
Gellert Global is represented by the Liberty Justice Center, the same legal group that dealt a major blow to Trump's trade agenda by successfully contesting his "reciprocal" tariffs.

The Supreme Court struck those tariffs down in February. The administration is in the process of refunding the estimated $166 billion that the federal government collected from importers through the reciprocal duties.
The Liberty Justice Center is currently engaged in two other lawsuits against what it says is Trump's misuse of laws to impose sweeping tariffs.

"This case is not about the president. It is about the presidency," the group's CEO Sara Albrecht said in a statement Tuesday morning announcing Gellert Global's suit. "No president should have the power to pull a dormant statute off the shelf and use it to impose sweeping tariffs or import bans without the limits Congress required."
The White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on the suit.

articles.title: SpaceX earnings live updates: Here's why analysts are bullish ahead of the report

paras.en: SpaceX is set to announce third-quarter results after the bell on Tuesday, the second earnings report for Elon Musk's defense tech conglomerate since its record IPO in June.
Here's what analysts are expecting, according to LSEG consensus estimates:

While SpaceX is best known for its reusable rockets, most of its revenue and profit in recent quarters came from the company's connectivity segment, which consists of its Starlink satellite internet service.

Buzz is building about Starlink's plans to build a U.S. mobile network after SpaceX, earlier this month, announced that it's buying 800 MHz of low-band spectrum, and after the Federal Communications Commission approved a plan for the company to build out a 15,000-satellite constellation.

The moves strengthen "Starlink Mobile's ability to compete with major carriers by enabling broader, deeper coverage," RBC Capital Markets analysts wrote in a note ahead of earnings. The firm has a $225 price target on SpaceX stock and the equivalent of a buy rating.
In the third quarter, analysts are expecting AI revenue of $6.47 billion, connectivity sales of $4.84 billion, and revenue in the space business of $1.41 billion, according to StreetAccount.
During the third quarter, SpaceX also closed its $60 billion purchase of AI coding startup Cursor.

articles.title: If Elon Musk gifts SpaceX stock through Trump Accounts, it will come with a catch

paras.en: Elon Musk said on Monday that he will give every kid in America a share of SpaceX next year. He appeared to suggest the gift could land in Trump Accounts — thanking Brad Gerstner, an architect of the program, for "helping enable this" in a comment on X.
But if the shares are distributed through the new investment accounts for children, the gift could come with significant strings attached.

Musk's announcement comes weeks after the U.S. Department of the Treasury rolled out guidelines for stock donations to Trump Accounts, also known as 530A accounts. Those include restrictions on selling donated stock: Children who receive it generally cannot sell for five years, even if the company runs into financial trouble.

Treasury's temporary regulations, subject to revision after public comment, aim to encourage stock gifts. But they also give donors unusual influence over children's investments, according to lawyers and philanthropic experts who spoke with CNBC.

In the broader world of charitable giving, donors can typically express preferences about how their gifts are managed, but the receiving organization or trustee retains final authority, said Carolyn Schenck, an attorney and former national fraud counsel at the IRS.
Under the new Trump Account rules, however, it's "the donor that's dictating the terms of the gift," she said.
Representatives for Musk, Gerstner and the Treasury Department did not respond to CNBC's requests for comment on the proposed gift.

According to the Treasury, about 70 million Trump Accounts have been created, including more than 60 million through a recent auto-enrollment effort. Trump Accounts are available to all children with U.S. citizenship under age 18 with valid Social Security numbers.

Musk would be the second philanthropist to publicly announce a stock pledge to Trump Accounts: SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell pledged earlier this summer to use the Trump Account program to gift some 2 million shares. That gift has not yet been distributed.
Trump Account beneficiaries do not have the latitude to sell under circumstances that other investors might otherwise.

Under the new rules, families cannot refuse stock gifted to Trump Accounts and generally cannot sell it until the earlier of five years or the end of the calendar year in which the beneficiary turns 17. Before then, early sales are permitted only in limited circumstances, such as certain corporate transitions or when the stock is formally delisted from a national securities exchange — not when financial or legal problems emerge that could prompt an investor to sell.

"Giving families more choices and more ability to hold the assets that they think are best for them and their kids' future ... would be a good thing," said Adam Michel, director of tax policy studies at the Cato Institute, a libertarian think tank. "But this is not really that, because you have no choice in the asset that is being deposited into your child's account, and then you also have no ability to sell it for the five-year holding period."
The temporary regulations also mandate that if any gifted stock is sold too early, the trustee must purchase the same number and class of shares "as soon as practicable."
This increases beneficiaries' risk of loss if the share price rises before the trustee repurchases the stock, according to Schenck. Beneficiaries would ultimately bear that cost.

"If the fiduciary makes an investment mistake, then the focus is typically restoring value to the beneficiary. But here, the focus seems to be restoring the specific security itself," said Schenck, who left the IRS in 2025 for law firm Caplin & Drysdale.
CNBC has learned the buyback provision is intended to quickly correct trading errors, though the regulations do not explicitly state that purpose or limit the requirement to accidental sales.

The temporary regulations cite donor interests. According to the text, "Donors are attracted by the hope that a stock contribution with a five-year holding period may lead recipients and their families to feel that they have a stake in the fate of the corporation."

Restricting sales virtually eliminates the risk for donors and their companies that Trump Account recipients will sell gifted shares en masse, liquidating a large enough position to depress share prices, according to Jane Ditelberg, chief tax strategist at Northern Trust.
"Certainly, for people who have highly concentrated wealth in a company, and the assets are sitting in their own personal pockets, this makes it a lot easier to give," she said.

Generally speaking, donors can get a bigger tax benefit by gifting appreciated stock to charity than donating cash, as they can claim the charitable deduction and avoid capital gains tax on the gains.

A Treasury official told CNBC that the rules are intended to build long-term wealth for children, especially in lower-income families, and encourage donations. "The major donors we've engaged are motivated by a desire to help children build generational wealth and get a head start on their financial future," the official said in a written statement.
Treasury has said it is in discussions with Trump Accounts donors ranging from "small to mega," but has not identified additional stock pledges since Shotwell's July announcement.
CNBC has identified fewer than a dozen pledges from philanthropists, though about four dozen major employers have committed to seed accounts for their employees' children.

In documents explaining the temporary rules, Treasury pointed to Michael and Susan Dell's $6.25 billion cash pledge and unspecified "similar donations," while acknowledging uncertainty about whether that level of giving will continue. "It is unclear whether this level of giving can be sustained in the long run or whether it is concentrated as Trump accounts are launching," the text states.

Trump Account funds generally may be invested only in low-cost index funds and exchange-traded funds. In the temporary regulations, the Treasury said directly contributed stock is different because it doesn't use account funds for the purchase.

But Ditelberg said a court could conclude that requiring an account to retain individual shares is still an investment decision — an argument that may carry more weight after the Supreme Court's overturning of Chevron deference. Because of the 2024 ruling, courts no longer have to defer to federal agencies' interpretations of statutes when the language is unclear.

"These accounts are going to have to stay invested in those stocks, and the question is whether that's directly contradicting the terms of the statute," she said. "I can't tell you how a court would rule, but I could say there's room for a challenge here."
Ditelberg added that state law grants the right to disclaim an asset. She said it's unclear how the Trump Account donation procedures would accommodate that right.
Schenck noted that Treasury has broad authority to set the terms of Trump Accounts, and it is Treasury — not the original stock donor — that formally requires the shares to be held.

The arrangement also differs from traditional charitable giving. For example, donors who contribute stock to donor-advised funds can recommend how the assets are managed, but the sponsoring charity retains ultimate control, including the authority to sell the shares. This is required to meet the IRS's legal standards for taking a tax deduction on a charitable contribution.

"A key principle is that the charity must have genuine control over the donated assets, including the ability to determine when to sell them, for the gift to qualify as a completed charitable contribution," said Gil Nusbaum, chief administrative and legal officer of National Philanthropic Trust.
Experts say the broader question is whether Treasury's approach aligns with the law Congress enacted.

"Musk's gift would be incredibly generous, but it doesn't change the fact that Congress intended these accounts to be diversified," Michel said. "It wouldn't be a bad innovation for Congress to allow tax-free gifts of appreciated assets, but changes to the law should come from Congress, not by administrative fiat."

articles.title: The Selfish Gene at 50

paras.en: Fifty years ago Richard Dawkins, a young and relatively unknown ethologist at the University of Oxford, published what would become an instant bestseller and the catalyst for his ascension as a prominent public intellectual. As its title suggests, The Selfish Gene argued that evolution is driven by selfish competition among the “fundamental particles” of inheritance: genes. The book arguably did more than any other since Charles Darwin’s On the Origin of the Species in 1859 to make evolutionary biology a hot topic of cultural conversation.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Its message seemed stark, and it still sparks controversy. We are, Dawkins argued, merely the “survival machines” of our genes, compelled by them to act in ways that promote their own interests. As those interests are selfish, so we, too, are “born selfish.” What looks like altruistic behavior, then, is merely in the service of our genes’ selfishness.

“It’s such an extraordinary book,” says evolutionary biologist Arvid Ågren, author of The Gene’s-Eye View of Evolution. “It has come to play a unique role in evolutionary biology—simultaneously influential and contentious.”

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

The “gene’s-eye view” of evolution introduced by Dawkins remains a central feature of modern evolutionary theory. But what that perspective reveals about the relationship of genes and organisms is still debated. One problem is that there’s no consensus about what a gene even is. “‘Gene’ is one of those words in biology that means different things in different corners of the field,” Ågren says. And whether genes are truly selfish depends on what you consider them to be.

Dawkins defined a gene in his book as “any portion of chromosomal material which potentially lasts for enough generations to serve as a unit of natural selection.” That’s not an easy sentence to parse, but it makes the gene an abstract entity defined by its evolutionary role. The definition wasn’t really Dawkins’s, as he acknowledged; other evolutionary biologists, in particular Bill Hamilton, George Williams, John Maynard Smith and Robert Trivers, had introduced the concept years prior.

But when we hear today that a gene is linked to, say, the risk of a disease, the word has a rather different meaning. Here it generally refers to a small stretch of the DNA that constitutes our genomes, typically one that encodes the chemical makeup of a protein molecule. To a developmental biologist, such a gene is a resource that cells use to make and maintain the organism. But to an evolutionary biologist, a gene is like a little agent that develops strategies over the course of evolution to ensure its own persistence.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: These are very different entities, although they are connected. The evolutionary biologist doesn’t much care what a gene does, so long as it somehow affects the traits and thus the fitness of the organism. The developmental or molecular biologist doesn’t much care how a gene got to be the way it is but wants to know how it influences growth, cell function and health. And so these disparate camps may find themselves talking past each other. The question that hangs over The Selfish Gene is whether, by failing properly to acknowledge the distinction—some might even say by obscuring it—the book sowed confusion about genes.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “At the heart of this confusion lies a disciplinary conceptual divide,” says developmental biologist Alfonso Martinez Arias of Pompeu Fabra University in Spain. Evolutionary, molecular and developmental biologists all have different concepts of the gene, he says. “Dawkins only thinks about the evolutionary biology view and has little knowledge, and certainly no understanding, of molecular or developmental biology.” Reviewing The Selfish Gene in 1977, molecular biologist Gunther Stent said that Dawkins’s definition “denatures the meaningful and well-established central concept of genetics into a fuzzy and heuristically useless notion.” Dawkins, Stent said, had committed a “terminological misdemeanor” quite deliberately “to provide himself with a catchy title.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: To make matters even murkier: whether you believe genes act selfishly depends not only on which kind of “gene” you’re talking about but also on what you take “selfish” to mean. In The Selfish Gene, “there are at least four [different] uses of ‘selfish’ that we glide between,” Ågren says.

For example, Dawkins says that two “genes” could compete for the same slot on a chromosome. But these are generally regarded as variants of the same gene, called alleles. If we’re speaking about alleles, selfishness seems an apt metaphor. As Dawkins says, an allele that results in an organism with longer legs to escape predators will be more likely to survive from one generation to the next, and so it will tend to become more abundant in a population’s gene pool. That is, this “long-legged” allele multiplies at the expense of others that are less fit. Kind of selfish, right?
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Then again, every distinct gene in a given genome must generally cooperate with the others if the host organism is to exist at all. Naturally, Dawkins recognizes this too. In his 2024 book The Genetic Book of the Dead, he even showed a mock-up cover of The Selfish Gene with the title changed to The Cooperative Gene, which, he said, would have been equally consistent with the book’s content. But if a word works as well as its antonym, what explanatory work is that metaphor actually doing?

The problem is that the gene that is “selfish” is not the same gene that is “cooperative.” A gene encoding one kind of protein, for instance, doesn’t really act selfishly toward a gene encoding a different protein, because their interactions are not a zero-sum game. Indeed, they probably need one another.

The real point of Dawkins’s first book is not that (evolutionary) genes are necessarily selfish, even metaphorically, but that they can be considered from an evolutionary perspective to enact strategies that enable their persistence. That makes these strategizing genes sound like wily little agents. But in considering how genes act to build and maintain an organism, they are generally nothing of the sort, not least because DNA itself is inert. It’s only over many generations that this illusion of strategic agency becomes evident. As long as we remember that this pseudoagency is purely metaphorical, there’s no problem—but invoking it (as Dawkins has) to strip actual organisms of their genuine agency is problematic, to say the least. His portrayal of organisms as passive vehicles driven by agentic genes is a fair description of the gene’s-eye model of evolution. The trouble is, this image doesn’t do justice to what organisms really are and do.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: A focus on what any given model leaves out can cut both ways, however: occasional “selfish” gene conflicts really can occur. For example, genes on the sex chromosomes (X and Y in humans) can act in their own favor to skew sex ratios in a population. What’s more, there are some segments of our DNA that really do seem to act with a selfish desire to proliferate at all costs. These are typically transposons—remnants of virus DNA that can accumulate in host genomes over time. Across many generations the build-up of transposon DNA that plays no beneficial role in the health of the host organism can clog the genome and compromise the fitness of other genes. This really is “selfish DNA,” although such sequences are not in general really genes in the developmental or molecular sense as they don’t affect the traits of the organism. Instead they are often given the more neutral label “selfish genetic elements.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Such truly selfish DNA has long been of interest to evolutionary biologists, and work on it by Trivers was a major influence on Dawkins when writing The Selfish Gene. Some biologists interpreted his book as proposing that all genes have this sort of selfishness. If that were so, the “selfish gene” hypothesis would seem now disproven in general. Most of our DNA that serves some useful biological function is best regarded as cooperative.

Among experts, then, the perception of the book’s core meaning still varies based on discipline. Some will say it’s about competition of alleles; some will say it’s about selfish genetic elements; some will say it’s just a metaphor (but for what?); and some will say it simply means genes don’t care about one another (which is just another metaphor and is, in any event, not what “selfish” means).

That Dawkins’s book is written so beautifully perhaps disinclines most readers from worrying about such distinctions. But is that a problem? Given that understanding what genes are and what they do is more important than ever in our modern age of gene editing, genomic selection of embryos and an alarming resurgent interest in eugenics, the legacy of The Selfish Gene on its half centenary is complicated. Some researchers feel that its evolutionary message remains illuminating, while others, like Martinez Arias, worry that it has sown confusion about what our genes are really up to.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: All this is to say that despite (or even because of) its myriad interpretive confusions, The Selfish Gene is still relevant. Debates over its fertile and provocative perspective are still shaping evolutionary biology and attracting newcomers to the field. It was and remains an “invitation to evolutionary biology that triggered the imagination,” Ågren says. “I was very seduced by that as a teenager.” But he cautions that, as with any science book, “if this is the only thing you read, you’ll be shaped by it, and you’ll think that’s the state of the field.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: In some respects, he says, pondering the meaning of Dawkins’s magnum opus is similar to wondering about the purpose of an evolution-sculpted genome itself: “To make the most of it, you must understand what it was designed to do.” And if the central metaphor has withered as we have come to understand more about the genome and about what genes really do, that is, after all, how science works: by proposing ideas that stimulate research until giving way to something better, more accurate, more true.

articles.title: Green stars do exist—and others shine pink or purple, too

paras.en: One of science’s greatest strengths is its capacity to learn from mistakes. Confronted with an error, a good scientist will admit to being wrong and use the new information to learn even more.

In my January 16 The Universe column, I wrote that there are no green stars. This is because a star’s temperature governs the mix of colors of light it emits, and the way our eyes perceive that mix tips the colors to either side of the green part of the spectrum so that stars appear mostly white, blue, orange and red. The sun actually gives off most of its light in blue and green, but a variety of factors influence our perception of its color, making it appear white or perhaps slightly yellowish.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
But can a star be just plain ol’ green? Nope. And I’ve been saying so for years.
WD J133001.13+643523.7 would like to have a word, however. And that word is “chartreuse.”

The white dwarf star—let’s just call it J1330 for short—really has a greenish tint, according to some interesting research published in the journal Royal Astronomical Society Techniques and Instruments on October 15. Astronomers used real observations, together with calculated models of white dwarf spectra, and, using sophisticated techniques, converted them to approximations of what our eyes would see. Surprisingly, these odd stars come in a range of delightful hues, including, yes, even green in the case of J1330.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The important change over my earlier claim is that different kinds of stars emit light in different ways. Normal stars like the sun—those still fusing hydrogen into helium in their cores—are gigantic balls of very hot ionized gas. Material in this state generally emits light across the entire visible spectrum, spread out smoothly across the rainbow of colors, from blue to red. When each color’s brightness is graphed against its wavelength, the plot (called a blackbody curve for historical reasons) resembles a lopsided bell curve that peaks at a given color, depending on the star’s temperature. Hot stars peak in the blue, cooler stars do so in the red. Some emit more green or yellow, or what have you.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Normal stars also have a thin atmosphere of ethereal gas surrounding them. Material in this gas can absorb colors at very specific wavelengths, creating dips in the blackbody spectrum. This can affect the overall color of the star—by making it slightly bluer, say, if the dilute gas preferentially absorbs red light—but the effect is minimal in essentially all cases. That is, a star’s color is completely dominated by its temperature rather than these second-order atmospheric effects.

White dwarfs, however, are different. These are compact objects that used to be the cores of stars like the sun; when a sunlike star dies, it blows off its outer layers, revealing its inner heart, which slowly cools in space over the eons like an ember from an extinguished fire. This ultradense sphere (a cubic centimeter weighs a metric ton!) is fiercely hot and holds about half the mass of the sun crammed into a volume only about that of Earth. This means white dwarfs have tremendous surface gravities, with a typical value being about 100,000 times Earth’s! Standing on the surface of a typical white dwarf, I’d weigh about 6,800 metric tons—equivalent to over 200 fully loaded semitrucks. (Did I say, “Standing”? I meant, “Squashed into a millimeter-thin smear of vapor.”)
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: That intense gravity means white dwarfs can have much thicker atmospheres than a normal star—thicker but squatter: most of a white dwarf’s atmosphere only reaches centimeters in altitude above the surface. But it can be very dense, on the order of a gram per cubic centimeter (about the density of liquid water). The white dwarf’s gravity is so strong, in fact, that atoms and molecules in its atmosphere can be squeezed so hard that a condition arises called “pressure broadening,” in which gas absorbs a wider range of colors than it otherwise would. All this means a white dwarf’s atmosphere can be much more efficient than a normal star’s at absorbing light emitted from below.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Combining all this information, the astronomers who did the new research examined the colors of quite a few real white dwarfs to see how they’d look to human eyes. The results were a shock to me! Some “white” dwarfs, it seems, are instead yellow, pink or purple.

Or, yes, as demonstrated by our friend J1330, they can even be green. It’s more of a chartreuse, but that counts. So there does appear to be an actual green star. And where there’s one, more are bound to exist, even if we haven’t seen them yet.

I’d love to have a good true-color image of J1330, to be honest. Unfortunately it’s a very faint star, and a decent-sized telescope would be required for the task. Even then, getting the color balance of an image right is tricky. Still, it would be fun to see it.

And I’m kicking myself; at some point I actually considered the idea that selected absorption in a stellar atmosphere might tip a star’s emissions enough to make it green but dismissed this because I was only thinking of normal stars! I’m glad these astronomers were more clever than I was.

There’s another, darker aspect to this as well. Although dense, the surface of a white dwarf is technically a fluid. The ridiculously strong gravity means that heavy elements tend to sink rapidly into the white dwarf’s interior, leaving lighter elements (such as hydrogen and helium) on the surface. Other elements, such as sodium, should readily disappear, yet that’s the exact element that makes J1330 look green! How can it exist in the atmosphere at all?
White dwarfs, it so happens, are astrophysical zombies that will happily destroy and consume their own planets.

Long after a sunlike’s star demise, some of its planets might drop down too close to the remaining white dwarf, where its ferocious tidal forces can tear them apart, shredding them into rubble. Earth has a relatively high abundance of sodium in its crust, for example, so it’s not a stretch to think rocky exoplanets should, too. Asteroids and even comets have sodium in them as well, so there’s quite a supply. If there’s a semiconstant stream of material falling onto the white dwarf, that could explain the supply of sodium that turns the tint up.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: While this “polluting” of the atmosphere is a relatively common phenomenon, it takes just the right mix of planetary chunks and white dwarf temperature to produce a star that looks like J1330. So while I will happily admit to being wrong in my earlier declaration, at least one thing I said remains correct:
For stars, it’s (still) not easy being green.

articles.title: Scientists left in the dark by National Science Foundation grant application delays

paras.en: A major federal grant program that helps researchers purchase scientific equipment has seemingly gone dark, leaving scientists unsure of whether they will be able to apply for funding.

The National Science Foundation’s (NSF) Major Research Instrumentation (MRI) program provides funding for the development or acquisition of state-of-the-art, often expensive equipment that researchers use to perform fundamental science and engineering experiments. These could be for kits such as clusters of GPUs to power research into artificial intelligence, which can run into the millions of dollars to buy and install, or highly specialized lasers or microscopes. Grant applicants can ask for up to $4 million, and they must demonstrate that the equipment will be used by several groups or experiments—a condition that can make the submission process more complicated than for other grants.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: In a statement released last year, the NSF said it planned to accept submissions in 2026 between October 15 and November 16. But the proposed opening date, October 15, has come and gone.

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

It’s the second year in a row that MRI applications have hit a speed bump. In 2025 the NSF suspended applications for the 2026 fiscal year. The agency said it had an enormous backlog of meritorious proposals from the previous year that it would consider funding instead.

When asked for comment, an NSF spokesperson said the agency is “currently working to update this funding opportunity,” but did not confirm to Scientific American when the submission process might open.

The delay comes amid numerous shakeups to federal funding of science. The Trump administration has cancelled numerous grants that had already been granted through the NSF, the National Institutes of Health and other agencies, and has attempted to introduce a major overhaul that would have granted sweeping oversight of grants to political appointees rather than the panels of experts currently in place. That change was temporarily halted in a recent government bill but could be reintroduced in December. The Trump administration has said these changes have been conducted in the name of promoting “gold standard science.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Several people involved in submitting MRI grant applications say they have received no word from the NSF as to when the submission period for this year might open. Laura Rodman, a grant proposal consultant, says she was told by a contact at major grant consultant firm McAllister & Quinn that proposal solicitations would start shortly after the federal government’s new fiscal year began on October 1.

The lack of clarity on when, or if, the submission period will open is leaving U.S. universities and research institutions in the lurch. One grant specialist at an American university who asked to remain anonymous to protect their privacy says schools are often limited in the number of MRI grants they can apply for. In turn, universities often run their own internal, highly competitive submission process before applying—a time-consuming effort for researchers and their labs.
“Nobody knows when the deadline will be or if it will even happen, so the act of planning to apply is a gamble,” the specialist says. “Are these faculty wasting their time?”

Even the simplest grant proposal may require up at least 30 to 40 hours of preparation, according to one scientist, who also asked to remain anonymous because they currently have a proposal pending at the NSF. That workload is increased for MRI grants, because of the need to show high levels of collaboration between research teams.

“Grants are very competitive, so an investigator must write the strongest argument they can for why taxpayer funds should go to their project,” the scientist says. “Scientific instrumentation is expensive, and the NSF wants to see that a new instrument will be used regularly. Many MRI requests involve four to six scientists, which increases the coordination needed to write a compelling proposal.”
The fact that the grants are written for groups of scientists means that a delay in the submission process can ripple out and affect multiple research projects.

“If you have a broken $700,000 instrument, or an instrument that is rapidly approaching the end of its useful life, a delay could have significant consequences,” the scientist says. “Researchers may put their projects on hold, or worse, waste money on Band-Aid repairs when a replacement would be far more efficient.”
“Moreover, sometimes a few months can be the difference between a high-impact publication and getting scooped,” they add.

The delays are particularly acute given the rising concerns about the U.S. falling behind international competitors in STEM fields; the NSF is a major funding source for critical research fields, such as chemistry and physics, the scientist says.
“For researchers without National Institutes of Health funding, the MRI program is often the only available option,” they add.

articles.title: Horned dinosaurs’ weapons evolved to handle the forces of combat
articles.author: Jake Buehler

paras.en: Triceratops’ massive skulls were built for horn-to-horn grappling. The rhino-like Centrosaurus could withstand stabbing its nose horn up and down. And the parrot-faced Psittacosaurus would have been wise to avoid a fight: Its head was ill-suited to handle blows.

New simulations using 3-D models of the heads of five different horned dinosaurs reveal what forces the skulls could withstand in battle. The results provide insight into how these dinosaurs evolved to use their face-based armory in combat, researchers report September 24 in PeerJ.
Ceratopsians — horned dinosaurs like Triceratops — have been hypothesized to use their imposing headgear as armaments for battling with other members of the species.

Fossilized facial injuries consistent with head-to-head violence have provided physical clues. “We know from many fossils that ceratopsian skulls tended to get banged up a little bit … in very particular spots on the frill or on the cheek,” says Andrew Farke, a paleontologist at Raymond M. Alf Museum of Paleontology in Claremont, California. But little else was known about how ceratopsians actually used their horns in battle.

Studying the biomechanics of the animals’ weaponized skulls could provide information on what movements and forces the dinosaurs evolved to tolerate. Such biomechanics research had previously been done on the bite stresses of theropod dinosaurs like Tyrannosaurus and on the forces felt by the club tails of armored dinosaurs, says vertebrate paleontologist Eric Austin Ames Jr.

Ames and his colleagues at the University of Bristol in England developed digital 3-D models of six skulls across five ceratopsian species spread across the group’s evolutionary tree. They simulated the combat stress experienced across the skull, varying the direction of attack and how the weaponry was used. Higher stresses in the skull meant a greater risk of mechanical failure, Ames says. The dinosaurs are more likely to have evolved to fight in a way that was well-tolerated by the skull’s mechanics.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The team found that early members of the group from about 125 million years ago — like the hornless, husky-sized Psittacosaurus — didn’t have skulls well-suited for combat of any type. The pig-sized Protoceratops had a skull that tolerated ramming fairly well. Larger, later-diverging species like Centrosaurus and the three-horned Triceratops and Spiclypeus appeared adapted to a wider range of combat styles.

Centrosaurus may have been a specialized stabber, lunging its head to jab at opponents. “When we tested [the skull] with vertical forces, it actually handled the stresses really well,” Ames says. “But when we tried side-to-side, it did not perform very well.”In contrast, Triceratops and Spiclypeus had skulls that tolerate the forces generated by interlocking horns and wrestling.

Ames thinks ceratopsians’ horns and frills probably first evolved for social and sexual display, but were soon used for full contact purposes. “Throughout their evolutionary history, their [horns’ traits] started to really explode in diversity and that coincided with different intraspecific combat styles,” he says. “This is something we see in modern herbivores.”

Much like with the antlers and horns of modern deer, buffalo or antelope, these weapons could have easily been turned on predators as well. “These adaptations are kind of like a Swiss Army knife,” Ames says. “They can be used for multiple things.”

The team created its 3-D models from surface scans of fossilized skulls. More detailed models that better simulate the complicated internal structure of these dinosaurs’ immense, bizarre skulls could provide even more insight to this prehistoric fight club, Farke says.

articles.title: AI can give you your voice back
articles.author: Laura Sanders

paras.en: When people face losing the ability to talk, they need alternative ways to communicate. One way people preserve their voice is by banking it. The process has improved in recent years, but it still produces a voice that can sound unnatural. Jules Rodriguez did this as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS, left his own voice diminished. But he wasn’t happy with the sound.

New technology that uses artificial intelligence allowed Jules to create a voice clone, one that sounds like his old voice. With breaths, intonations and even stutters, these voice clones capture the quirks of a human voice. Jules’ voice clone was so realistic that his wife cried the first time she heard it.

In this episode, hear how AI-powered voice clones are changing the conversation around how people connect. That includes a musician named Patrick Darling who uses his voice clone to sing and perform songs.
Laura Sanders: Jules Rodriguez’s voice was disappearing.
Jules Rodriguez: For me, it felt like I was fading away, like when Marty McFly was seeing his family fade away in the picture he had in “Back to the Future.”

Sanders: Jules has ALS, and like many people with that disease, this fading felt inevitable. But there was something Jules could do about it. I’m Laura Sanders, and this is episode three of The Deep End: Talk To Me, a Science News podcast on the human voice and all it can hold.
[voices] Hey mom, can I tell you something? The voice is absolutely an integral part of your identity. Do you want to talk? That added layer of it being you. Hello? Your voice. Hi.
Sanders: On today’s episode, we’re going to hear about the return of Jules’ voice.

We touched on this in the last episode, but as a reminder, there are a few traditional ways people preserve their ways to communicate when they’re faced with losing a voice. One is for people to record themselves saying common or special phrases if they can still talk. That’s called message banking. And then there’s a technique called voice banking. It requires a person to record themselves saying very specific words. And then these sounds get fed into a computer program that can stitch them together to make any word a person wants to say. Sounds good in theory, but in practice, the output didn’t sound very human. Jules banked his voice soon after his diagnosis. MA describes what that was like.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: MA: I remember both of us looking at each other while he was recording, basically the old school way, and they still recommend to bank your voice this way, besides your cloned voice, but you’re sent all these phrases that you’re just recording, like 350 phrases, and that goes into, you know, a file, and then when you do need it, the company will pull it up and plug it into your device.
Sanders: I spoke with Richard Cave. He’s a speech therapist at University College London who works with people with ALS. That’s also called motor neuron disease, or MND.

Richard Cave: My role was to build out the voice banking initiative across the UK. This was back in 2017. And I remember… After the first, I don’t know, six months, nine months, being very proud that I managed to put through 100 people or so at an average duration to complete the voice banking, all 1,600 phrases in around three months each. Very proud of that. They weren’t awful, but they weren’t good. And they didn’t really represent the person. They represented kind of part, a little bit, of the person. But that was the best we had.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Having decoded the signals from some input device, such as the switch, one then has to broadcast it in a form people can understand. This could be visually, with text or diagrams on the screen. But if you want to communicate like others, which is what people in my position would like, you need to speak.
Sanders: The late physicist Stephen Hawking had one of perhaps the most iconic computerized voices. Here he is giving a talk in 1994 at MIT.

[Hawking audio] Computerized speech synthesizers have improved a great deal in recent years, and this is important. Not only does one want to be understood, but also one doesn’t want to sound like Mickey Mouse or a Dalek.
Sanders: He’s describing his synthesized voice, which it turns out, he quite liked.
[Hawking audio] This voice of mine may be a bit tinny and Irish, but it is almost human.
Sanders: Hawking was happy with that voice. Jules was not. Jules described his banked voice in a stand-up routine as sounding like if you played Daft Punk at quarter speed.

[Sanders voice clone] Okay, fast forward a bit, artificial intelligence came onto the scene. Now, with just short snippets of already recorded sound, these powerful programs can create synthetic voices with appropriate umms, breaths, sounds, and cadence that are very close to the original. These voices are so realistic that sometimes you can’t even hear the difference.

Sanders: Maybe you just noticed something, but maybe you didn’t. Those previous three sentences weren’t spoken by me at all. They were said by a voice clone I made. Okay, one more time. This is me talking.
[Sanders voice clone] And this is my voice clone.

Sanders: I used ElevenLabs to clone my voice. That’s a company that uses AI technology to create lifelike, digital replicas of voices. To do it, I used the professional option, which required 30 minutes of audio to make. So for input, I recorded myself reading a few podcast scripts.
Jules Rodriguez’s voice was disappearing.
Sanders: Some really long texts from my mom.
I’m at Food Lion. I’m getting pickles, half and half.
Sanders: And chapter nine of Anne of Green Gables.
It’s a good thing Rachel Lynde got a calling down. She’s a meddlesome old gossip.
Sanders: After a few minutes, poof, there it was, my voice clone. It was spooky how much it sounded like me. I spent a fun afternoon playing with it. You can control so many different parts.

[Sanders voice clone] It can speak quickly. And it can speak slowly. My voice clone can laugh. It can be utterly bored. It can also scoff when it thinks something is ridiculous. It can be menacing on Laura’s behalf.
Sanders: I could even speak fluent French.
[Sanders voice clone] Il peut même parler d’autres langues.

Sanders: The technology uses a few different types of artificial intelligence at different stages. It extracts features of my voice, such as my pitch and tone, my prosody, even my breathing patterns. This lets it build a model of my voice, and then that model can be let loose to say anything I type. I got the idea from speech pathologist Kate Nilson, who has tried it herself.

Nilson: We’ve even played the game of like, is it really me talking or is it the computer? And it’s kind of scary how realistic the computerized version of my voice is. The really awesome part about the voice cloning process is that you take recordings and submit that. It’s not like you record it right now. You take old recordings. And so for people you know for instance people living with ALS, if their speech is the first thing that’s affected and their speech has already changed, it might be too late to do the recordings, but if they have old voicemails or a speech that they gave or a podcast that they were on, something like that, then we can take those recordings and submit them to make a voice. And so that’s really opened a lot of doors for a lot of people.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Sanders: In June of 2024, Jules used recordings of his own voice to create an AI-generated voice clone, also through the company ElevenLabs.
Jules: When I first heard my cloned voice, it felt like I reappeared. When my wife first heard it, she cried because of how close it sounded like me before I lost my voice.
Sanders: After months of gradually hearing Jules’ voice less and less, his family had gotten used to the new normal. The voice clone was a big change.
Jules: They were all shocked at first, but now it just feels natural. It’s pretty crazy.
Sanders: When you first started using the voice clone, do you remember what the first thing you said was? Were there things you really wanted to say?
Jules: Well, it was probably the cheesiest thing. I remember telling my wife how much I love her.
Sanders: Here’s how his wife MA remembers it.

MA: The first thing he played for me, I was like chills all over. And it was, it was incredibly beautiful and incredible and like, wow. And also I cried because it felt like there was a part of him that I was getting back that I had lost a long time ago.
Sanders: It was surprisingly hard to get this one thing back in the middle of so much loss.

MA: It felt confusing emotionally to get that part back and not the rest of him back. Like, I just I feel it right now in my body as I talk about it. Things with ALS change so quickly and the voice is something so intimate you’re sort of like, you’re training yourself little by little to adapt and then all of a sudden this like really vibrant part of him came back, but everything else was the same. But that vibrant voice part came back and it was like, yeah. It was a bizarre experience but ultimately really, really special for us and for his son too.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Sanders: Jules immediately took off the training wheels.
Jules: I just wanted to explore the limits of it.
Sanders: In fact, Jules’ voice clone sounded so good that he decided his dream of doing stand up comedy was possible, long after he had given up the idea.
Jules: I started to write jokes with it pretty soon after hearing it.
Sanders: So Jules started working on a set.

MA: When he tested the AI voice, it’s like a little light bulb went off and he was like, I think I could do comedy again. And I remember hearing that and going like, oh, my God, like that’s such a huge like thing to, to, it’s like you come alive in a new way, is what I saw through his eyes. He was like, I think I can do comedy again. I was like, wow.

Jules: Oh, man, thank you. I wasn’t even sure if I was going to make it out here. So many things could stop me from being here. Hospital stays, tracheostomy, broken elevator. And the biggest thing would be any step larger than two inches. I’m so happy to be here with you all.

Sanders: It’s tempting to think that this personalization shouldn’t matter much, that having a voice, any voice, would do the job. But it’s not true. Having a voice that sounds like your real voice does matter a tremendous amount.

Karina Nagin: You need to communicate what you’re thinking, your health directives. You need to tell your loved ones you love them. But I think we didn’t realize what a huge impact your voice sounding like you, what a big piece of identity that was.

Sanders: Karina Nagin directs Bridging Voice, a nonprofit organization that helps people with ALS find and use communication technology. That includes voice clones from ElevenLabs. It’s the group that helped Jules clone his voice. She’s heard stories about how voice clones and the connections they bring back led people to reconsider their medical directives.

Nagin: And people, once they received these voice clones, it was so life-altering that they were changing their health directives of what they wanted to do. Many people changed their health directives. They said, if I have this voice and I can sound like me, I can continue to communicate and feel like myself, I want to live longer. This is something that makes it worth living for me. I think our team didn’t realize how impactful it was going to be, but we’ve had people use these voice clones to tell their wedding vows. I got a testimonial from a grandmother the other day who just got her voice clone, and she said, I immediately called up my grandchildren, the youngest of who had never heard my real voice. And so this is the first time they were hearing my voice.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Sanders: Nagin says her team was surprised by the impact on not just the person whose voice is restored, but on their families too.

Nagin: We were so focused on people and giving them the ability to communicate. The idea that it sounds more like them or not, we said, oh, that’s a nice add-on, but that’s not really the core of it. But as soon as we gave that to people, we realized that is the core of it, your identity and feeling like yourself. And it’s not just for the patients, but it’s their family members.
Sanders: A personalized voice, one that sounds like the old one, is more than an add-on.

Nagin: Endless videos of people. I mean, we have one of a college-aged boy who’s hearing his father’s voice for the first time in two years, and he just breaks down. Like, this is, you know, they’re going through this horrific experience of this diagnosis. And to be able to actually connect with a family member and hear their voice again, I think it equally brings joy and comfort to the families as much as it does to the person who’s been diagnosed with ALS.

Sanders: ALS forces families to confront tough medical decisions about life and death. Jules and MA had thought very carefully about how they’d approach the future. What kind of medical interventions would he be OK with, and what kind would he not want? Big picture, what sort of life was worth living? Jules had been getting by with just an external oxygen mask to help keep his body going. He had decided that he didn’t want to take a next big step of having a tracheostomy, a life-extending procedure that leaves a small tube in his throat connected to a ventilator. With a trache tube, Jules would need round-the-clock care, and he would lose his voice permanently.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: MA: He was someone who didn’t want to do a tracheostomy. Like, he was opting for, once I’m done, like, that’s it. And that was our plan.
Sanders: In the summer of 2024, not too long after he had cloned his voice, Jules had reached a very tough spot.

MA: September, we went to the hospital again and we had one evening where we really thought like that was it, like he was going to, he was going to pass away that night. I remember texting his family and saying, you know, I don’t know that it’s going to happen right now, but we’re, I feel like we’re really close. And he went through this like crisis moment. And then on the other side, when they were able to like stabilize him again, he looked at me and he was like, babe, well, if the tracheostomy can help me live, then I think I’d change my mind. I want to do it. Let’s talk to the doctors about it.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Sanders: This decision to have a trache tube placed in his throat meant that Jules’ voice, diminished as it already was, would be gone. Remember, this is a couple who built their relationship on long, deep talks. Their intimate, funny, thoughtful conversations were so meaningful to them that they started an entire podcast based on them. But this decision, a proactive choice to fully and permanently lose the capacity to talk, represented a hard stop. A definitive end to talking. What you’re about to hear is a tough conversation. MA is telling me about a moment before the surgery.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: MA: So I remember the night, the day, yeah, he was, the operation was like in the evening when they did it, and me recording like a last little video of us talking because I was like, I just want to capture your voice one more time. And he was like, oh babe, you know, being all like, and I haven’t even looked at that video, but it’s there. And so that was a big, it was a big transition.
Sanders: You can’t see it, of course, but maybe you can hear it. As we talk, we’re both crying.

MA: I think I mentioned when we spoke last time how of all the things from the very beginning that I was like, oh, he’s going to lose the ability to this and this and this and this and this. I was like, oh, my God, when he loses the ability to speak, like, I’m going to really, really, really, really, really have a hard time. And all of the abrupt changes and the way you have to adapt to them kind of prepare you for the next things. And so usually the fear of the thing happening is more than when it actually happens. And then you’re there and you’re like, okay, we’re here and we’ll adapt to it. That’s usually been the case for pretty much everything. But yeah, it was big.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Sanders: But there was something that made the final and complete loss of Jules’ voice easier. Jules’ new digital voice. This was a very realistic AI-generated recreation of his old voice, the one that his family knew and loved. The existence of this new voice factored into Jules’ decision to get a trache.
MA: I really do believe that the AI voice and the ability for him to actually communicate in that way is one of the things that helped him decide to keep living.
Sanders: It wasn’t everything, of course. A decision like this depends on so many moving pieces. But it was big.

MA: I firmly believe that it had an enormous positive impact in him considering it, like, as a way of you know having certain goals and experiences that he thought, you know, wouldn’t have been there, had it not been for the cloned voice. So I’ve I’ve gone as far to say that if it wasn’t for the clone voice, I don’t think he, I don’t think he would have chosen the trache. Yeah, then that moment anything could happen, but he was pretty, a pretty like no, I don’t want the tracheostomy kind of guy from the beginning. And then all of that changed. And so I think it was a huge driver.

paras.en: Sanders: At the time of Jules’ hospitalization and surgery, they talked to their son Skylar about what was going on.

MA: The whole like communicating with him afterwards, because I said, you know, now he’s going to lose his voice completely. He’s like, we have the computer. That’s great. And I was like, okay, yeah, true. The things he’s told us over time are like bonkers. How he sees, the perspective he has on things, is incredible. So that was a really big, pivotal time for like what it means to like use your voice, to keep your voice, to fight for your voice and to express yourself in ways that you didn’t even think you would before. That takes a lot of courage and willingness.

paras.en: Sanders: And what is your voice? I mean, to Skylar, it didn’t matter because his voice was still there.
Sanders: To Jules’ son, the voice clone was his dad’s voice. That’s really all there was to it.
MA: He had his tracheostomy October, October 1st, and he was in the hospital for another two weeks. And then, mid-November, he was performing at, you know, an improv at one of our local comedy clubs.
Jules: In all seriousness, thanks for coming out. My name is Jules and because of the advancements in AI, I now have the ability to come up here and do this again with my original voice.
Sanders: Jules was back. Jules, with his voice clone, can laugh and sing and start trouble with his wife.
Jules: One thing in particular is how it inserts tone and inflections on words. Sometimes my wife will get mad because my response can come off with some sass.
Sanders: I asked Jules if he can swear with it.

Jules: [Beep] yeah, I can. With the latest version of this technology, I have more control of how I sound with prompts. That includes laughing, whispering, and even singing. I could never sing, even though my wife and I met at a karaoke bar.
Sanders: I think you can sing. Anyone who wants to sing can sing.
Sanders: Cave has been a speech therapist for decades, but even he was won over by the capabilities of these newer AI-generated voice clones.

Cave: I was really pleasantly surprised. These voices were the most authentic sounding I’d ever heard from this technology. It actually sounded like the people I was working with. And so it really changed my world. And because I was known for voice banking, I was getting a lot of inquiries. And I ended up spending so much time on answering questions about ElevenLabs. What really, really excited me was that many people reported that their social networks was being strengthened again, that more people were coming to talk to them and to reflect on times past and times current. And that to me is gold. That’s what voice banking is or should be, to maintain social and work networks.

paras.en: Sanders: I’d say that we’ve now gone well beyond almost human, as Stephen Hawking put it. Today’s voice clones are fluid, individual, and in many ways, seamless. My synthetic voice says certain words the exact same way I would say them.
[Sanders voice clone] My real voice says certain words the exact same way I would say them. It’s spooky.

Sanders: The stories I’ve heard of how people are using these voices back this up. I emailed with Peggy Merrill, who lost her voice from ALS. She uses her voice clone to read to her grandkids, teach yoga, and lead guided meditation.

Sanders: Peggy wrote to me, “It renews my sense of self to use and hear my own voice.” And there’s Patrick Darling, who you heard from in an earlier episode. He’s a composer and musician, and he’s been writing new songs and performing them with his voice clone.
Patrick Darling: The first time I performed with the AI voice, I was surprised how physically connected I felt with it, even though I was not actually singing.
Patrick: It’s hard to explain. There’s just this strange energy about it and you feel like a performer again.

Sanders: Patrick’s description of feeling physically connected to his voice, I think, might be a big hint about why this voice cloning technology is so powerful. These realistic voices are able to create connections both within people and between people. These connections were lost, and then they’re remade. And they matter because of not just the big heavy conversations, but the little everyday stuff too.

Jules still has to use eye-tracking technology to type out what he wants to say. He has a device that senses where he’s looking on a screen and uses his gaze to write. Only then does his voice clone say what he wants it to say. That takes a lot of time and focus. Scientists are working on ways to get the words out faster by using signals earlier in the speech process.
On the next episode…researchers want to pull words straight from the brain.
Casey Harrell: And the more I read and I thought, why not me? And why not now?
Sanders: What does it feel like to have your thoughts turned into words?

Leigh Hochberg: The first thing that he said was something along the lines of, you know, is this thing on? And then the second thing that we decoded was, I’m looking for a cheetah.
